videos.title: EXCLUSIVE: Cruel Santino On Alternative Music, Industry Reset & Why The System Does Not Sustain Art
videos.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Cruel Santino On Alternative Music, Industry Reset & Why The System Does Not Sustain Art
videos.description:
Cruel Santino is not holding back. In this exclusive interview on the Morning Rush with Osi and Eve, he opens up about the alternative music scene, the industry reset and why the system is not designed to sustain people who put art first. "I don't think the system is necessarily designed to sustain people who put art first," he says. He talks about the lack of infrastructure for alternative artists and why risk takers are finding it harder to take creative risks.

He also speaks on Afrobeats going global and why Nigerian artists need to focus on their home base. "A lot of Nigerian artists forget to develop where they are from and pay a lot of focus to maybe where it pays them the most." He references the Dancehall era and how Americans eventually went back to their traditional R&B and pop. "If we follow historical patterns, they have always consumed music from everywhere else." He believes artists need more individual substance and authenticity. "You have to be overly authentic right now."

The conversation also touches on his new project KLCB, Kings of the Bounce. He explains the album cover and the world he created. "It's like James Bond meets Final Fantasy. It's tech coded." He speaks on the features with Jeriq, Mavo and Ziggler the 10th. "Just friendship. Features are a lot more organic now." He also reveals that Big Drop is not necessarily the lead single. "There are so many lead singles. I balanced everything from every side of me on this project." And he talks about his Boiler Room performance for Christmas. "It's going to be an experience."

videos.title: EXCLUSIVE: Mr. Eazi On Saving Afrobeats, Chop Life Empire & Why Talent Is Not Enough
videos.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Mr. Eazi On Saving Afrobeats, Chop Life Empire & Why Talent Is Not Enough
videos.description:
Mr. Eazi is not holding back. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, he makes a bold claim. "I saved Afrobeats in 2016." He talks about the state of the genre back then and how he stepped in to give the people something. But now he is back and he is doing it one more time for the culture. "10 year anniversary. Give thanks to God."

He also opens up about his business ventures. Empower is transitioning into Chop Life, his Disney that wraps up all his entertainment businesses. He speaks on signing new artists like Mr. Eazi and the success they are seeing. "Mr. Eazi put out the first single in October. Smash!" He also talks about Locker Room Bonus, his initiative to build data infrastructure for sports in Nigeria. "It is not CSR. It is selfish. If you want to put money into sport, the data has to be there." Division 2 League players get paid straight to their locker room. No FA. No club. Straight to them.

The conversation also touches on the music. He speaks on his collaboration with Moliy for the song Molly. "She is one of the most talented artists period." He reveals how the song came together, from the sample to the flight from Accra to London. He also talks about his legacy. The Evil Genius album. Accra to Lagos. Lagos to London. And why he had to step back and let his brothers shine. "Let your brother shine." The great philosopher Shea Vibes said it. And Mr. Eazi lived it.

videos.title: Shine TTW Opens Up: Lagos Move, Lover Boy Truth & Why He Keeps Fans Waiting
videos.headline: Shine TTW Opens Up: Lagos Move, Lover Boy Truth & Why He Keeps Fans Waiting
videos.description:
Shine TTW is not holding back. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, he opens up about his journey from Anambra to Lagos, moving before he was 18 and why he had to leave home to chase his dreams. "When your dreams are bigger than your environment, you have to go," he says. He talks about the strict parents who wanted him to be a doctor and the day he told his father he could not do it. "I'm smart enough to be a doctor if I choose to. But I don't want to."

He also speaks on being recognized by Apple as Up Next for Nigeria in 2024. "It was a huge milestone. It made me believe that anything is possible. From sleeping and waking up in the studio, not knowing how we even get to the studio the next day." He sees milestones as a battery to keep going. "It's like a battery to keep going. Energize." And he talks about doing the groundwork. "I believe I'm the kind of artist that when everything starts, I've taken time out to do the groundwork."

The conversation also touches on his single Addicted. "It's a lover boy aspect of me. No need for long stories. Let's get to the loving." He speaks on promotion and why putting out music without it is child's play. "If you don't have 50 million to put your song on TikTok, you have to be the 50 millionaire now." He references Molly's Check It To The Max and how she posted 200 videos. "That is the only way you can actually break the norm." And he reveals what is next. "One or two singles, then we'll talk about the project. Keep them waiting. Keep them guessing."

videos.title: Yemi Alade Opens Up: Self-Titled Album, Beauty Line & Why She Named The Project After Herself
videos.headline: Yemi Alade Opens Up: Self-Titled Album, Beauty Line & Why She Named The Project After Herself
videos.description:
Yemi Alade is a force and she is not slowing down. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, she opens up about her self-titled album, her beauty line YEM Beauty and why she has always stayed true to herself. She talks about working with Don Jazzy on the video and how she could not keep a straight face. "My face was not straight. I laughed from beginning to end. Don Jazzy himself is such an epitome of blessing. He is so funny."

She also speaks on the new generation of female artists. Tyla, Fave, Tiwa and more. "The females have always just been waiting for this opportunity. And I fear that we are coming in." She gives credit to platforms like OC that share the music of females. "We need more of that in the media space where females are given the opportunity to share their music just because they are musicians, not because of their gender."

The conversation also touches on her album. Titanium is a mashup of R&B, highlife and disco. "I did not spare my vocals." She dreams of having Bruno Mars on it. "I feel like the energies would be so in sync." She also talks about her love for French Africa and France. "I go where the love is." And she reveals that she put out the album title to her fans. "I did not name this album. I put it out to the audience. And the name that kept reoccurring was a self-titled album. It's like a little love note to the fans."

•  Why service (not just the game) drives the Chess in Slums work
•  Full-circle moment returning to Cool FM after the Chess Is Lunch project

In a generation hungry for authenticity, one voice rises like a tide that refuses to be boxed in. This is the story of An Endless Ocean — an artist who draws from the infinite depths of faith, the tender machinery of love, and the liberating truth that “who the Son sets free is free indeed.”
From the first notes of Nazarene that made listeners ask “Who is this guy?” to the twin 2026 projects Love Is a Machinery and the 14-track Freedom, An Endless Ocean has crafted a sound that is unapologetically his own. •  Why he refuses the typical gospel mold and simply makes music from life experiences (faith, love, and everything in between)
•  The intentional crafting of his unique sound and the slow, genuine acceptance that followed
•  The two-year journey behind dropping two full albums back-to-back
•  Collaborations with Ryan Ofei, Wale Adenuga, Bolu Ajayi, Seylan and more
•  The meaning behind his name, the importance of staying true to himself, and the growing global reach of Nigerian gospel

•  His message to the community that has become family
Whether you’re discovering him for the first time or you’ve been singing along since Hexagon, this interview is a window into the heart of an artist who believes God is the endless source — and that there’s room for every genuine expression of that truth.

videos.title: Basket Mouth Interview: Yabasi 2 Launch, Star-Studded Features & Legendary Stories
videos.headline: Basket Mouth Interview: Yabasi 2 Launch, Star-Studded Features & Legendary Stories
videos.description:
Basket Mouth is a legend and he is not holding back. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, he opens up about Yabasi 2, his creative process and why he does not force artists on records. "I don't force an artist on the record. I listen to the music until the music calls for the artist." He talks about the making of the album and how he told Dr. Seth to leave any artist that gives stress. "Any artist that is a bit difficult, that gives us stress, when it comes to jumping on this record, let's leave the artist."

He also speaks on his approach to music. "When I decided to enter the music space fully, I wasn't going for respect. I just wanted to make music. Evergreen sounds, evergreen music." He talks about the layers of Yabasi and why the album is called Yabasi, which means onions. "Everything about the album has so many layers." He also tells the story of how he got the beat for Yabasi from Dr. Seth after two years. "Give me that beat. Five minutes later, Wizard Chan had it. One hour later, I had this song."

The conversation gets emotional when he speaks on Sound Sultan and the song Feel It, the first posthumous appearance from the legend. "When I heard my guy's voice, my eyes filled with tears. That was it." He also talks about working with Ikechukwu, Johnny Drille and the rest of the star-studded lineup. And he shares wisdom for young artists. "Hang with the real ones. Don't expect too much from anybody. And try not to feed too much from social media."

videos.title: Seun Kuti - The Working Nepo Baby, Na Dem, Fatherhood, Coachella Freestyle & Naming the Real Enemy
videos.headline: Seun Kuti - The Working Nepo Baby, Na Dem, Fatherhood, Coachella Freestyle & Naming the Real Enemy
videos.description:
In a world where the global elite own the platforms, the narrative, and the attention, Seun Kuti — son of Fela, leader of Egypt 80, and self-described “nepo baby who still has to work” — refuses to coast. He clings to ordinary moments (school runs, mall trips, organizing his daughter’s life) to stay grounded amid a wild, dream-like existence filled with wilder people.

His brand-new six-track album Na Dem (released November 6) is the latest chapter in that story. Pieced together over two years by stealing studio days across Lagos, London, Paris, Rio de Janeiro, and Los Angeles while on the road, the album is a masterclass in live Afrobeat that refuses to soften its message. The title track began as a spontaneous freestyle at Coachella that went viral long before its official release. Features include Tom Morello’s revolutionary guitar on “Na Dem” and Kabaka Pyramid on “Problems.” Tracks like the deeply personal “Adara” (named after his daughter, meaning “it will be well”), “Real Life,” “DJB (Devil Just Busy),” and “As How” blend intimate hope with sharp calls for reflection.

In this unfiltered Cool FM Breakfast Show conversation with Manny and Vanessa, Seun opens up about the cost of staying true to his message, why he prefers exclusion over the old-school retribution of his father’s era, the difference between seeking reaction versus reflection, and why music is cooperation — not competition. It’s the portrait of a man who knows what is happening, knows it is bad, and uses his music to give people the courage to face it instead of escaping it.

videos.headline: From Digable Planets to Harvard: Ladybug Mecca's Next Chapter (Audio Only) | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
The Digable Planets icon on Blowout Comb, her Harvard fellowship, and tracing hip-hop's Afro-Brazilian roots.

Before Digable Planets helped redefine the sound of alternative hip-hop, Ladybug Mecca was a young artist absorbing Brazilian music, jazz, and the rhythms of her family's home. Three decades after Blowout Comb became a cornerstone of jazz-inflected hip-hop, the pioneering MC joins Donwill to discuss her latest chapter as a recipient of Harvard University's Nasir Jones Hip-Hop Fellowship. Her research traces the connections between hip-hop and Afro-Brazilian traditions, from Candomblé drumming to capoeira, challenging the idea that hip-hop simply arrived in Brazil rather than finding a culture already connected through rhythm, movement, and shared African ancestry.

Ladybug Mecca reflects on her Brazilian parents, the influence of MC Lyte and Queen Latifah, and the enduring relevance of Digable Planets' Blowout Comb. She opens up about navigating hip-hop as a young woman, her friendships with Guru and Bahamadia, her collaborations with Prince Paul and Brookzill!, and why documenting Black creativity is increasingly urgent in an era of cultural erasure. Still an avid music discoverer, Mecca also shares her excitement for a new generation of women MCs and explains why her next creative chapter is as much about recovering history as making it. Ladybug Mecca breaks down:

- How the Nasir Jones Hip-Hop Fellowship is helping her investigate connections between Afro-Brazilian culture, hip-hop, and the Black Atlantic.
- Why the Blowout Comb continues to resonate across generations and how “Black Ego” has taken on new meaning amid cultural erasure.
- Collaborating with Prince Paul on Brookzill!, building friendships with Guru and Bahamadia, and hearing her voice sampled on Snoop Dogg's “Candy.”
- Why archival research, music discovery, and the rising generation of women rappers remain central to her creative life.

videos.headline: Fola Interview: Football Dreams, Davido/ Drake Dream Collab & Why He Believes Anything Is Possible
videos.description:
Fola is not your typical lover boy and he is setting the record straight. In this exclusive interview on the Midday show with Abi, he opens up about his new album, his approach to love songs and why he does not rush things anymore. "I know how to narrate love stories very well," he says. "I'm not much that deep of a lover boy like that."

He talks about his song My Type and how it is really a body positivity anthem. "Whatever sort of body type you have, you're beautiful just the way you are." He also speaks on his brotherhood with BNXN and whether an EP together is possible. "BNXN is my brother. Shout out to BNXN." He even reveals that he used to play football actively until he broke his arm. Would he have been a richer footballer than an artist? "I know how to sing more than I know how to play football."

The conversation gets deep when he talks about success and faith. "You can't tell me that nothing is impossible. That's just what I know." He believes Nigerians limit themselves and it is his responsibility to show people that anything can happen. He also reveals he would love a Fola and Drake song and has even written something for it. "When your dreams are too big, they laugh at you."

He also breaks down how 2am in Toronto came together. He recorded it a while ago, stumbled upon it in his archives while on tour in Canada, and reached out to OBO Baddest who picked it and sent it back the same night. The rest is history.

videos.title: Founders Chat: How Gabriella Uwadiegwu and Flora Uwadiegwu Built Wetech as Sisters
videos.headline: Founders Chat: How Gabriella Uwadiegwu and Flora Uwadiegwu Built Wetech as Sisters
videos.description:
In this founders chat, sisters Gabriella and Flora Uwadiegwu tell the story of building @Wetechng  together. Before this non- profit focused on opening doors for women in Africa’s tech ecosystem, Gabriella was 19 standing in a room of 25,000 women in tech at the 2017 Grace Hopper Conference in Orlando, Florida. She left asking why a room like that only existed in the US. It took eight months for her to find the first 50 women for the first Wetech conference, with potential investors telling her no one invests in women. Her brother told her to build anyway. A few years later, their small team of three planned a 1000-woman conference, and grew to include an entrepreneurship track after Gabriella’s own struggle to raise money led her to start investing her savings. 

Gabriella and Flora discuss being the only Black girl in the room, attending coding bootcamps, why women have to aim past equality, and how building an organization together changed their relationship as sisters.

videos.description:
The R&B icon takes Donwill inside his musical upbringing, Babyface's mentorship, and the hip-hop collaborations that helped shape Cool Relax.

Before Jon B. became one of the defining voices of '90s R&B, he was a kid surrounded by records, instruments, and a family of classically trained musicians. In this episode of the Almanac of Rap, the singer, songwriter, and producer traces his journey from teaching himself piano and drums to meeting Babyface and Tracey Edmonds, signing his first record deal, and releasing his debut album Bonafide. What began as a dream of becoming a behind-the-scenes songwriter and producer evolved into a recording career after Babyface encouraged him to step into the spotlight. Jon B breaks down:

- Meeting Babyface and Tracey Edmonds: The unexpected audition that turned a young songwriter's ambition into an artist deal, the making of Bonafide, and the enduring lesson Babyface taught him about honesty in songwriting.
- The golden age of '90s R&B: Why Tony! Toni! Toné!, Jodeci, Boyz II Men, Guy, Blackstreet, and other groups influenced his songwriting, production, and approach to rhythm.
- Inside the Native Tongues and Soulquarians orbit: Visiting Q-Tip's studio, learning MPC techniques from J Dilla, and receiving encouragement from the artists who inspired him.
- Recording with Guru: How Ali Shaheed Muhammad helped create the Cool Relax remix, why Guru's late-night studio session became unforgettable, and the inspiration behind its futuristic desert music video.

videos.title: Saul Williams on Leap Life, the Politics of Art & the Power of Poetry | The Almanac of Rap
videos.headline: Saul Williams on Leap Life, the Politics of Art & the Power of Poetry | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
What happens when an artist refuses to separate creativity from revolution? Poet, musician, actor, filmmaker, and cultural provocateur Saul Williams joins Donwill for an expansive conversation about Leap Life, his first solo studio album in seven years, and Songs My Mother Taught Me, a new nonfiction book examining the experiences and ideas that shaped his political consciousness. 

Working alongside producer Carlos Niño, Williams transforms experimental soundscapes, dance rhythms, and ancestral memory into music that confronts artificial intelligence, colonialism, and the machinery of modern power. From recording a track inside Cairo's bustling streets on his leap-day birthday to hosting listening séances honoring the lives lost to violence, Williams reveals why his latest work is both deeply personal and unapologetically political.

Saul travels with Donwill back to the Brooklyn poetry scene of the 1990s, where Williams shared open-mic stages with future cultural luminaries, including Yasiin Bey and Erykah Badu, before becoming a defining voice of the spoken-word movement. Saul breaks down:

- The making of Leap Life: How Carlos Niño helped transform years of experimental demos into a cohesive album.
- The ideas behind Songs My Mother Taught Me, the influence of Paul Robeson and W.E.B. Du Bois, and why Williams believes music should challenge power rather than reinforce it.
- His first performance at Brooklyn Moon Cafe in 1995, friendships with Yasiin Bey and Erykah Badu, and the creative community that helped bring spoken-word poetry to a new generation.
- His journey through film, theater, and experimental storytelling, including Holler If Ya Hear Me, his years in Paris, and the patience required to create work that defies categorization.
- The relationship between AI and forced labor explored in "Robot Slave," his listening séances, and why fiction, poetry, and music remain essential tools for imagining liberation.
